reason: The article concerns UK cinema music tariffs, not Suno-assisted creation or release decisions.
Live Nation’s proposed investment in a Chilean concert promoter does not inform the series.

This RSS-discovered MBW article reports Suno’s statement that v6 training included user creations and distinguishes that statement from Sony and Universal’s allegations and Suno’s response. It can inform piece 03 on what creators should verify about submitted work. Suno has a commercial stake; the litigation allegations are not findings, and Suno’s September 9 launch is background. The company statement remains one underlying claim wherever repeated.

The Italian Competition Authority’s October 6 primary statement identifies the Suno terms it is investigating. It informs piece 03’s terms checklist for the stated Italian consumer-law context. An opened investigation establishes neither unfairness nor a violation; the applicable terms version still needs checking before publication.

Serj reports measurements from three songs generated with the same lyrics and prompts across model versions, plus WAV/MP3 comparisons available for two songs. Piece 02 can use the observed loudness and peak differences and the small-sample limit. These measurements do not establish aesthetic quality or typical v6 behavior; the author also runs the publishing blog.
A UMG executive’s departure offers no specific evidence about Suno’s workflow, output, or creator release decisions.
Believe’s regional leadership appointment adds no information about its Suno partnership or creators’ use of Suno.

This RSS-discovered Los Angeles Times article includes original interviews with musicians, a songwriter representative, Suno’s product chief, and others about consent and undisclosed payouts in AI licensing deals. Piece 03 can distinguish their concerns and company responses from established outcomes. Label deals do not themselves prove an individual artist’s consent or future payment; the reported lawsuits remain allegations.

MBW reports Deezer’s announced search filter for fully AI-generated music, which could affect how a released track is found. Piece 03 can identify it as a planned platform change. Deezer’s detection and fraud figures are its own claims and do not establish how a particular Suno-assisted song will be classified.

MusicRadar’s original interview records Todd Edwards describing how he generates material in Suno Studio and samples it in his production. Pieces 01 and 02 can use this identifiable practitioner workflow and his creative judgment. His assertion that the resulting material is entirely his and free of lawsuit risk is not established; the publisher discloses affiliate links.

Suno’s October Studio release note specifies downbeat detection, clip stretching, fade curves, and floating windows. Piece 01 can report these as announced workflow changes. Suno markets its product, and its claims of smoother timing or reduced manual alignment are not independent performance tests.

Dazed’s original interviews record Kilo Kent and Zemi describing Suno vocal modification within songs they say they otherwise make, and report their label’s attempt to vet the article. Pieces 02 and 03 can use these attributed accounts to examine control and disclosure. Their production histories and degree of human input are not independently demonstrated; both artists and their label have commercial stakes.

The ytyng author documents 24 v6 generations, settings, export formats, and spectral measurements against 12 earlier tracks. Piece 02 can examine the observed results alongside the author’s disclosed differences in songs, prompts, codecs, and uncertain earlier model versions. The measurements cannot prove v6 sounds worse, and the proposed licensing-to-quality explanation is unsupported speculation.
The sponsored Jaasu interview discusses production careers but provides no Suno use, test, or relevant release decision.
This TuneCore-supported interview concerns a live entertainment promoter’s business and does not document Suno-assisted music making or release.

Madverse’s founder describes its own AI distribution checks without identifying a Suno-specific practice or result. The company has a commercial stake, and this does not answer the series’ release questions.

The retained timestamped transcript records JG Beats Lab founder Josh’s proposed demo-to-arrangement workflow and his advice to retain demos, settings, stems, and vocal takes (seg-00118–seg-00174). Piece 03 can cite that practitioner passage as a documentation practice. His terms and ownership interpretations require primary-text and jurisdiction checks; he promotes his newsletter and studio work.

The retained timestamped transcript records the host making two songs from rough recordings and prompts, then describing both enjoyment and artifacts (seg-00016–seg-00053; seg-00076–seg-00085). Piece 02 can use this as one creator’s experience, not an audio-quality finding or representative test. The host’s speculation about training sources and legality is unverified.

The retained timestamped transcript documents one creator’s successive lyric-direction prompts, stated settings, and later Studio stem cleanup (seg-00137–seg-00203; seg-00390–seg-00426). Pieces 01 and 02 can examine the work involved and his reported control. He acknowledges that generation variation could explain the differences; the transcript alone cannot establish that vocals sounded better.

The retained timestamped transcript shows Andrea Olsen using one voice memo and a stated Suno prompt, then reporting which directions she thought the output followed (seg-00143–seg-00221). Pieces 02 and 03 can use the demonstration and her decision to limit what she uploads. One pass does not establish general model performance; her training, copyright, and Instant IP claims need primary verification, and she promotes an affiliate link and her commercial course.
